title: The Growth Plateau
summary: GrowthFlow is a growth-marketing automation platform for mid-market SaaS companies.

Q1.text: Growth has plateaued: monthly new leads are flat for 4 months despite increased ad spend. What do you do first?

choices.text: Segment lead growth by acquisition channel and customer segment
choices.reveal: LinkedIn ads drive 60% of leads at 8% conversion; Google 30% at 22%; organic 10% at 15%. The mix, not volume, explains the plateau.
choices.because: The aggregate number hides a channel quality story — volume is up but leads aren't converting.

choices.text: Audit the pricing page for friction in signup flow
choices.reveal: The pricing page has no friction — but it doesn't explain why LinkedIn leads aren't converting.

choices.text: Double down on LinkedIn ads since they drive the most volume
choices.reveal: Lead volume rises 12%, but conversion stays at 8%. The extra leads are still low-quality.

choices.text: Survey 10 recent leads who didn't convert to paid
choices.reveal: Three cite budget constraints, four mention competing tools, three say the platform doesn't solve their workflow. Suggestive but not conclusive.

Q2.text: LinkedIn drives 60% of leads at 8% conversion; Google 30% at 22%; organic 10% at 15%. What do you do next?

choices.text: Redesign onboarding to qualify leads before they reach pricing
choices.reveal: A qualification-first onboarding is scoped — but it adds friction for organic leads who convert well at 15%, potentially hurting that channel.
choices.because: Differential treatment per channel is the move that addresses the root cause without hurting organic.

choices.text: Shift budget from LinkedIn to Google ads
choices.reveal: Budget shifts — but Google ads are pricier per click, and reducing LinkedIn volume means total leads fall.

choices.text: Run A/B tests on pricing page copy for LinkedIn traffic
choices.reveal: Copy variations improve click-through by 3% but don't move conversion to paid. The issue isn't pricing page copy.

choices.text: Analyze lead quality by company size within each channel
choices.reveal: Small companies convert at 12%, mid-market 18%, enterprise 35% but only 15% of leads. The enterprise story is clear but the segment is underserved.

Q3.text: Survey responses suggest mixed reasons for non-conversion. What do you do to get clearer signal?

choices.text: Run a larger survey with a structured decision matrix
choices.reveal: The larger survey reveals three clusters: budget-constrained SMBs, mid-market evaluating alternatives, enterprises needing custom features.
choices.because: A structured survey separates the three use cases so each can get its own strategy.

choices.text: Offer a discount to the surveyed non-converters to recover the signal
choices.reveal: Discounts are offered — some convert, but the discount cohort's churn rate is 40% higher. You've acquired price-shoppers, not customers.

choices.text: Segment the original 10 responses by company size post-hoc
choices.reveal: Post-hoc segmentation finds a hint of patterns but the sample is too small to be actionable. More data is needed.

Q4.text: Enterprise leads convert at 35% but are only 15% of volume. Survey said budget-constrained SMBs, mid-market evaluating alternatives, enterprises needing custom features. What's your strategy?

choices.text: Double down on enterprise with a custom-tier offering, accepting lower total volume
choices.reveal: Enterprise is prioritized — but this means fewer SMB leads convert, and the volume drop means monthly recurring revenue falls 12% while deal size rises.
choices.because: This is the strongest move based on the evidence available.

choices.text: Build a self-serve tier for SMBs with limited features and a sales tier for mid-market
choices.reveal: Two-tier strategy is scoped — but it splits engineering focus across two products, and the SMB tier's low ARPU makes the growth math tight.

choices.text: Optimize LinkedIn ads to target enterprise decision-makers specifically
choices.reveal: LinkedIn targeting narrows to enterprise — lead volume drops 70% immediately, but conversion rate on the remaining leads improves. The growth curve inverts.

choices.text: Accept the plateau as market saturation and focus on retention
choices.reveal: Retention focus launches — but it doesn't address the new business stagnation.

Q5.text: You're considering onboarding redesign vs budget reallocation. Both affect channel mix. What's your priority?

choices.text: Build qualification-first onboarding that segments LinkedIn vs organic leads differently
choices.reveal: The onboarding redesign is scoped at 8 weeks — it qualifies LinkedIn leads with a use-case selector while fast-tracking organic leads. Post-launch, LinkedIn conversion rises to 14%.
choices.because: Differential treatment per channel is the move that addresses the root cause without hurting organic.

choices.text: Shift 30% of LinkedIn budget to Google ads and monitor for 30 days
choices.reveal: The shift runs — Google leads convert at 22% as expected, but the 30% volume drop from LinkedIn offsets the conversion gain. Net MRR is flat.

choices.text: A/B test qualification in onboarding and budget shift in parallel
choices.reveal: Two parallel experiments run — but the team splits focus, and results are harder to attribute.

Q6.text: You've scoped a self-serve SMB tier and a sales mid-market tier. What constrains the timeline?

choices.text: Engineering capacity — both tiers compete for the same team
choices.reveal: Engineering confirms both features hit the same 10-week timeline. Building in parallel extends delivery to 14 weeks. The roadmap choice is real.
choices.because: This is the strongest move based on the evidence available.

choices.text: Need to define the feature boundary between tiers
choices.reveal: The feature boundary workshop runs — but defining what's in vs out takes 3 weeks, delaying the launch window by a month.

choices.text: Need to hire enterprise sales to serve mid-market
choices.reveal: A search firm is engaged — but hiring a mid-market sales rep takes 3 months, so the sales tier can't launch until Q3.

Q7.text: Three paths have converged: enterprise focus, two-tier strategy, or onboarding redesign. Your lead engineer says the team can only execute two initiatives this quarter. What do you do?

choices.text: Rank the initiatives by projected impact and pick a coherent pair
choices.reveal: Based on projections: onboarding redesign ($41K MRR/month) + two-tier strategy ($38K) beat enterprise focus ($35K). You ship the onboarding redesign and scope the SMB tier, deferring enterprise.
choices.because: Ranking by impact and picking a coherent pair — both growth-plays, not an enterprise pivot — keeps the strategy aligned.

choices.text: Run all three in a compressed timeline by adding headcount
choices.reveal: Two new engineers are hired — but onboarding is delayed 6 weeks during ramp, the SMB tier ships with bugs, and enterprise focus never launches. Quality suffers.

choices.text: Let engineering pick which two they're most excited about
choices.reveal: Engineering picks the onboarding redesign and the SMB tier — the same choice you would have made, but without the impact rationale. The decision lacks strategic grounding.

Q8.text: You've shipped onboarding redesign and scoped the SMB tier. Month 1 shows MRR growth — but conversion on the redesigned LinkedIn flow is 12%, below the projected 18%. What do you investigate?

choices.text: Check whether the qualification criteria are too aggressive for mid-market
choices.reveal: The qualification screen filters out mid-market leads who would have converted — the 12% reflects only SMB+enterprise, but the SMB tier's features aren't ready yet to serve them.
choices.because: The qualification criteria filtered the very segment the SMB tier wasn't ready to serve — onboarding and product aren't aligned.

choices.text: Survey the 12% who did convert to understand their journey
choices.reveal: The 12% who converted praise the qualification flow — but they're the easiest sells. The survey doesn't explain why the rest didn't convert after passing the same screen.

choices.text: Attribute the shortfall to the SMB tier not launching yet
choices.reveal: The shortfall is attributed to the missing SMB tier — but the data shows the qualification flow is filtering mid-market leads who would have converted on the existing product.

Q9.text: The qualification flow filters mid-market leads who would have converted on the existing product. The SMB tier is still 4 weeks out. What do you do?

choices.text: Tune the qualification criteria to pass more mid-market leads while the SMB tier finishes
choices.reveal: The criteria are relaxed — mid-market leads flow through to the existing product tier. Conversion rises to 19%, above projection. Four weeks later, the SMB tier launches and criteria tighten back.
choices.because: Tuning criteria to match product readiness — loose while waiting, tight when the new tier is ready — captures revenue that would otherwise leak.

choices.text: Wait for the SMB tier to launch before changing the qualification flow
choices.reveal: The wait keeps conversion at 12% for 4 weeks — then the SMB tier launches and conversion jumps to 18%. The 4-week low-conversion window costs approximately $28K in foregone MRR.

choices.text: Remove qualification entirely and let the pricing page sort leads
choices.reveal: Qualification is removed — lead volume rises but conversion drops to 6%. Without upfront qualification, low-fit leads hit the pricing page and bounce at a higher rate.

Q10.text: You've tuned the qualification flow and the SMB tier launched. Three months show MRR up 22%. What do you measure next?

choices.text: Run cohort analysis on retention of leads through the new onboarding
choices.reveal: 3-month cohort retention for new SMB-tier leads is 62% — 4 points below the platform average.
choices.because: Acquisition is validated — but retention tells you whether the leads are good ones, not just more of them.

choices.text: Double down on the winning channel mix and increase ad spend
choices.reveal: Ad spend increases by 40% — but without a retention check, growing the top line without knowing if the new cohort churns faster.

choices.text: Declare success and shift the team to new initiatives
choices.reveal: The team shifts — but 62% retention on new SMB leads means the growth is less sustainable than it looks.

Q11.text: New SMB-tier lead retention is 62% vs 66% platform average. What do you do?

choices.text: Analyze the onboarding completion funnel to find where SMB leads drop off
choices.reveal: SMB leads drop off 30% more at the feature-discovery step — they see capabilities they don't need and get overwhelmed.
choices.because: The drop-off point is specific — feature discovery overwhelms SMB leads who need a simpler activation path.

choices.text: Survey churned SMB leads to understand why they left
choices.reveal: Surveyed churned SMB leads cite 'too complex for our needs' — but doesn't pinpoint where in onboarding the overwhelm happens.

choices.text: Assume the retention gap is natural and within acceptable variance
choices.reveal: The gap is accepted — but over the next quarter, churn compounds, and the growth trajectory falls below the plateau line.

Q12.text: SMB leads drop off at feature discovery — they're overwhelmed before reaching the aha moment. What do you do?

choices.text: Build a simplified activation path for SMB leads with guided feature discovery
choices.reveal: The simplified path is scoped at 6 weeks — it guides SMB leads through the core workflow and defers advanced features until value is proven.
choices.because: A guided path addresses the specific drop-off point — it doesn't remove features, just sequences them for SMB needs.

choices.text: Remove advanced features from the SMB tier entirely
choices.reveal: Advanced features are removed from SMB — but some growing SMBs need those features to justify an upgrade to mid-market. The tier becomes a dead end.

choices.text: Add a tutorial video and call it a day
choices.reveal: A tutorial video is added — but it adds cognitive load to an already overwhelming screen. Retention stays at 62%.

Q13.text: You've built a guided activation path for SMB leads. It's ready for rollout. But engineering raises a concern: the code path diverges from enterprise, creating maintenance debt.

choices.text: Ship the SMB path and plan a tech-debt sprint to reconcile the code
choices.reveal: The path ships — SMB retention rises to 68% in the first month. The tech-debt sprint is scheduled for next quarter, documented and tracked.
choices.because: Shipping the value with a known debt repayment plan is better than delaying — the benefit is proven before the cost.

choices.text: Block the launch until engineering refactors for a shared code path
choices.reveal: The refactor takes 3 weeks — but the SMB retention uplift is delayed, and the extra engineering time pushes the next feature two sprints out.

choices.text: Ship to 5% of SMB leads as a shadow test
choices.reveal: The shadow test runs — but 5% sample is too small to detect retention differences.

Q14.text: The guided SMB path ships, retention is up to 68%. The board asks: is this sustainable growth or a one-time correction? What do you tell them?

choices.text: Lay out the 6-month runway, the next 3 growth levers, and their projected impact
choices.reveal: The roadmap lays out: (1) SMB retention optimization (+$25K/month), (2) mid-market expansion (+$38K/month), (3) enterprise land-and-expand (+$45K/month).
choices.because: A 6-month runway with specific levers and projections gives the board confidence that the plateau break is the start of a trend.

choices.text: Report the 22% MRR growth and say the plateau is broken
choices.reveal: The 22% growth is celebrated — but without the roadmap of levers, the board questions whether the next quarters will show the same growth.

choices.text: Ask for 6 more months before declaring the plateau is broken
choices.reveal: The request for 6 more months is granted — but the growth team loses momentum, and two competitors ship similar features.

Q15.text: You've laid out the 6-month growth roadmap with three levers. But engineering says they can only staff one initiative per quarter. What do you do?

choices.text: Rank the three levers by confidence and projected ROI, fund the top one
choices.reveal: SMB retention (high confidence, $25K/month) leads, mid-market ($38K, lower confidence), enterprise ($45K, highest risk). You fund SMB retention for Q1.
choices.because: Ranking by confidence-adjusted ROI makes the staffing constraint a decision, not a crisis.

choices.text: Insist all three ship in parallel and escalate to the CTO
choices.reveal: Two contractors are allocated — but quality issues emerge across all three initiatives, and confidence signals get diluted.

choices.text: Ask engineering which one they'd most enjoy building
choices.reveal: Engineering picks mid-market expansion — but it's the second-ranked lever by confidence and ROI. The roadmap isn't grounded in business impact.

criteria.label: Letting evidence lead
criteria.guidance: Name the driver before betting the strategy.

criteria.label: Sizing customer impact
criteria.guidance: Ground the decision in what changes for the user.

criteria.label: Proving the outcome
criteria.guidance: Define the measure that validates the bet.
